headline: Frequent lows: 10.3% of readings below 70
summary: 65-year-old female, colorectal cancer, 1.8 years after treatment; normal at start; group: coaching + overnight fast; retired. Average sugar 83 mg/dL in weeks 11-12, 90% of readings in range. Median rise after dinner 37 mg/dL. ML forecast for a typical dinner: 43 mg/dL. Synthetic participant (made-up data).
plainSummary: This week: tell your care team about your low blood sugar readings. Ask if a diabetes medicine needs changing, and don't change your exercise or meal times until then.

careTeamFlag.rule: Send to the care team today if more than 1% of readings are below 54 mg/dL (level 2 lows). Send to the care team this week if more than 4% of readings are below 70 mg/dL, the average is above 250 mg/dL, or more than 5% of readings are above 250 mg/dL (sustained highs). Time in range under 70% alone goes to the next visit.

evidence.label: Time in range 70-180 mg/dL (weeks 11-12)
evidence.method: Share of 15-min sensor readings between 70 and 180 mg/dL.

evidence.label: Average blood sugar (weeks 11-12)
evidence.method: Mean of 15-min sensor readings.

evidence.label: Readings above 180 mg/dL (weeks 11-12)
evidence.method: Share of readings above 180 mg/dL.

evidence.label: Readings above 250 mg/dL (weeks 11-12)
evidence.method: Share of readings above 250 mg/dL.

evidence.label: Readings below 70 mg/dL (weeks 11-12)
evidence.method: Share of readings below 70 mg/dL.

evidence.label: Readings below 54 mg/dL, level 2 lows (weeks 11-12)
evidence.method: Share of readings below 54 mg/dL (consensus target under 1%).

evidence.label: Glucose management indicator (weeks 11-12)
evidence.method: GMI = 3.31 + 0.02392 x mean glucose; an estimate of HbA1c from sensor data.

evidence.label: Change in average blood sugar, weeks 1-2 to weeks 11-12
evidence.method: Mean of weeks 11-12 minus mean of weeks 1-2.

evidence.label: Status thresholds
evidence.method: alert: time in range < 70%, or > 5% of readings above 250, or > 4% below 70 (international CGM consensus targets). watch: time in range < 90%, or > 5% above 180, or average up 10+ mg/dL since weeks 1-2.

evidence.label: Meals with a clean sugar curve
evidence.method: Meals of 10 g carbs or more, with sensor readings and no other 100+ kcal item in the next 2 hours.

evidence.label: Typical rise after a meal (median)
evidence.method: Median of peak (15-120 min) minus pre-meal reading.

evidence.label: Typical rise after dinner (median)
evidence.method: Median of peak minus pre-dinner reading.

evidence.label: Dinners with a clean sugar curve
evidence.method: Scored dinners.

evidence.label: Dinners started at 8 pm or later
evidence.method: Share of scored dinners starting at or after 20:00.

evidence.label: Meals followed by a walk
evidence.method: Scored meals with walked_after_min > 0.

evidence.label: Your sugar rise after meals with a walk vs without
evidence.method: Your meals only, from the ML engine: what the meal predicts is removed first (gradient boosting, cross-fitted), then the walk effect is fitted on what is left; 95% CI from 300 bootstrap resamples of your meals.
evidence.caveat: You chose when to walk, so this is a pattern, not proof.

evidence.label: Best estimate for you (your data blended with the cohort)
evidence.method: Empirical-Bayes: 72.0% weight on your data, rest on the cohort estimate. People differed by about 6.9 mg/dL in this effect.

evidence.label: Your sugar rise after dinners at 8 pm or later vs earlier
evidence.method: Your dinners only, from the ML engine: what the meal predicts is removed first (gradient boosting, cross-fitted), then the late-start effect is fitted on what is left; 95% CI from 300 bootstrap resamples.
evidence.caveat: Late dinners may differ in other ways (what you ate, how tired you were).

evidence.label: Best estimate for you (your data blended with the cohort)
evidence.method: Empirical-Bayes: 64.0% weight on your data, rest on the cohort estimate. People differed by about 9.6 mg/dL.

evidence.label: Your average overnight fast
evidence.method: Hours from last bite to first bite, nights with sensor data.

evidence.label: Nights with a 13-hour fast or longer
evidence.method: Share of nights with overnight_fast_hours >= 13.

evidence.label: Program-wide: rise after meals with a walk vs without (same person)
evidence.method: Double machine learning: gradient boosting learns what the meal (calories, carbs, protein, fat, fiber, sugar, meal type) predicts about the rise and about whether you walked; the effect is fitted on what is left, within person. 5-fold cross-fitting repeated 3 times; person-clustered 95% CI.
evidence.caveat: Walking was self-chosen: association, not proof.

evidence.label: Program-wide: rise after a 10-19 min walk vs no walk
evidence.method: Double machine learning: gradient boosting learns what the meal (calories, carbs, protein, fat, fiber, sugar, meal type) predicts about the rise and about whether you walked; the effect is fitted on what is left, within person. 5-fold cross-fitting repeated 3 times; person-clustered 95% CI.

evidence.label: Program-wide: rise after a 20-29 min walk vs no walk
evidence.method: Double machine learning: gradient boosting learns what the meal (calories, carbs, protein, fat, fiber, sugar, meal type) predicts about the rise and about whether you walked; the effect is fitted on what is left, within person. 5-fold cross-fitting repeated 3 times; person-clustered 95% CI.

evidence.label: Program-wide: rise after a 30+ min walk vs no walk
evidence.method: Double machine learning: gradient boosting learns what the meal (calories, carbs, protein, fat, fiber, sugar, meal type) predicts about the rise and about whether you walked; the effect is fitted on what is left, within person. 5-fold cross-fitting repeated 3 times; person-clustered 95% CI.

evidence.label: Program-wide: rise after dinner at 8-9 pm vs before 6 pm (same person)
evidence.method: Double machine learning: gradient boosting learns what the meal (calories, carbs, protein, fat, fiber, sugar) predicts about the rise and about the dinner start time; the effect is fitted on what is left, within person. 5-fold cross-fitting repeated 3 times; person-clustered 95% CI. Night-shift workers excluded.

evidence.label: Program-wide: rise after dinners at 8 pm or later vs earlier (same person)
evidence.method: Double machine learning: gradient boosting learns what the meal (calories, carbs, protein, fat, fiber, sugar) predicts about the rise and about whether dinner started at 8 pm or later; the effect is fitted on what is left, within person. 5-fold cross-fitting repeated 3 times; person-clustered 95% CI. Night-shift workers excluded.

evidence.label: Program-wide: rise after dinner with a walk vs without (same person)
evidence.method: Double machine learning: gradient boosting learns what the meal (calories, carbs, protein, fat, fiber, sugar) predicts about the rise and about whether you walked; the effect is fitted on what is left, within person. 5-fold cross-fitting repeated 3 times; person-clustered 95% CI. Dinners only; night-shift workers excluded.
evidence.caveat: Walking was self-chosen: association, not proof.

evidence.label: Program-wide: rise after other meals with a walk vs without (same person)
evidence.method: Double machine learning: gradient boosting learns what the meal (calories, carbs, protein, fat, fiber, sugar, meal type) predicts about the rise and about whether you walked; the effect is fitted on what is left, within person. 5-fold cross-fitting repeated 3 times; person-clustered 95% CI. Breakfasts, lunches and snacks.

evidence.label: Randomized, people who started with normal: HbA1c change, coaching + overnight fast vs coaching alone
evidence.method: Difference in mean (week 12 - week 0) between randomized arms within this starting blood sugar group; bootstrap 95% CI.
evidence.caveat: Randomization holds within groups set at the start.

evidence.label: Randomized: extra overnight fast hours in the fast arm vs coaching alone
evidence.method: Mean overnight_fast_hours over all logged days, fast arm minus coaching arm.

evidence.label: Randomized: HbA1c change, coaching + overnight fast vs coaching alone
evidence.method: Difference in mean (week 12 - week 0) between randomized arms, completers; bootstrap 95% CI.
evidence.caveat: Fair comparison: groups were assigned at random.

evidence.label: Randomized: fasting glucose change, coaching + overnight fast vs coaching alone
evidence.method: Difference in mean (week 12 - week 0) between randomized arms, completers; bootstrap 95% CI.

evidence.label: Real-data check (CGMacros, 45 real adults): dinner at 8 pm or later vs earlier
evidence.method: Same ML engine as the program (double ML, calories and macros), within person; person-clustered 95% CI.
evidence.caveat: Same direction as the program data, but the interval includes zero: not proven in real people yet.

evidence.label: Real-data check (CGMacros): rise per extra MET of movement in the hour after a meal
evidence.method: Within-person, carbs adjusted; cluster bootstrap 95% CI.
evidence.caveat: No clear effect in 45 real adults over 10 days; Fitbit METs are a rough measure of walking.

evidence.label: Real-data check (CGMacros): rise after meals followed by a walk vs not
evidence.method: Walk = at least 10 straight minutes at 3+ METs (Fitbit) in the hour after the meal; meals with 50+ minutes of Fitbit data. Same ML engine as the program (double ML, calories, macros and meal type), within person; person-clustered 95% CI.
evidence.caveat: Check result: same direction, not proven. About 120 people would be needed to confirm an effect this size.

evidence.label: Real-data check (NHANES survivors, survey-weighted): HbA1c per extra hour of overnight fast
evidence.method: Survey-weighted regression adjusted for age and sex; design-based bootstrap 95% CI (PSUs within strata).
evidence.caveat: Check result: no clear signal. A one-time survey snapshot, not a trial.

evidence.label: Check: pre-meal sugar before meals that were later followed by a walk vs not (same person)
evidence.method: Negative control: a walk after the meal cannot change the reading 15 min before it. Same ML engine as the walk effect (double ML); person-clustered 95% CI.
evidence.caveat: Near zero, so walk meals do not start from a different place.

evidence.label: Check: how strongly a hidden factor would have to link to both walking and the rise to explain the walk effect away (E-value)
evidence.method: VanderWeele-Ding E-value; mean difference converted with the ML engine's within-person residual SD (20.1 mg/dL). For the CI bound nearer zero: 3.6.

evidence.label: Statistics cross-check (fixed-effects regression): rise with a walk after the meal, same person
evidence.method: Within-person linear regression (person fixed effects) adjusted for carbs and meal type; cluster bootstrap 95% CI over people. The advice uses the ML engine; this is the classic check.
evidence.caveat: ML engine: -17.8. The intervals overlap, so the number does not depend on the method.

evidence.label: Statistics cross-check (fixed-effects regression): rise with dinner at 8 pm or later, same person
evidence.method: Within-person linear regression (person fixed effects) adjusted for carbs; cluster bootstrap 95% CI over people. The advice uses the ML engine; this is the classic check.
evidence.caveat: ML engine: +9.2. The intervals overlap, so the number does not depend on the method.

evidence.label: ML forecast: expected rise after your typical dinner
evidence.method: Gradient boosting trained on every program meal (calories, macros, meal type, start time, pre-meal sugar and its trend, your usual rise). Each of your dinners is forecast by a model that never saw it (5-fold, out-of-fold); this is the average.

evidence.label: ML forecast: typical miss on a meal it never saw
evidence.method: Mean absolute error over 18218 out-of-fold meals; R² 0.62. 80% of misses fall between -20.47 and 22.35 mg/dL.

evidence.label: Randomized: do blood sugar groups differ in the fast effect on HbA1c? (test p-value)
evidence.method: Cochran Q across the three starting blood sugar groups (2 degrees of freedom). Under 0.05 would mean the groups really differ.
evidence.caveat: The program could not tell the groups apart, so advice uses the overall number.

recommendations.title: Tell your care team about low readings this week
recommendations.text: 10.3% of your readings were below 70 mg/dL and 0.0% below 54 (weeks 11-12); the usual targets are under 4% and under 1%. Low sugar can make you shaky or dizzy. Contact your care team this week rather than waiting for your next visit. Ask whether a diabetes medicine needs changing: insulin and sulfonylureas (glipizide, glyburide, glimepiride) are the usual causes of lows, and this data does not record medicines. Until then, don't change your exercise, fasting or meal times.

dataNote: Synthetic data from the Crane Lab hackathon set. Nobody in it is real.
